description.text: In Roman religion the Genio (plural Genii) was a tutelary spirit or nume that guarded the fortunes of families and individuals alike.  It was conceived as a benevolent presence that accompanies a person from birth, guiding their actions throughout life, much like a guardian angel.

The Genio was closely associated with the forehead, which was considered its sacred spot; worship involved touching the forehead as a sign of reverence.  It was often depicted as a serpent in art and inscriptions, and its influence extended beyond individuals to families, the state, provinces, and even the emperor, whose Genio became a public cult under Augustus.

curiosities.text: The Genio of a person is invoked on their birthday, the dies natalis, which was celebrated as the spirit’s own celebration.
The Genio was traditionally represented as a serpent, a motif that appears in Cicerone, Giulio Ossequente, and the lararium of the Vetti house in Pompeii.
Rome itself had a Genio, with a temple in the Forum near the Concordia temple, and the city’s Genio was sometimes described as either male or female.
The concept of a Genio extended to places, with the belief that no location was without a Genio (nullus locus sine Genio).
